newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee rally seen intact,supply weighs cocoa.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee rally seen intact,supply weighs cocoa.

text.p: A tight physical market and Brazilian frost fears are likely to bolster coffee prices through the third quarter, while cocoa sags on mounting supply.
Leading analysts, in commentaries available on Wednesday, also saw sugar as broadly balanced in 1996/97 but it was thought possible that it could feel a supply squeeze next year.
Earlier this month, the Green Coffee Association of New York said US stocks rose 111,000 bags in March.

"Considering the high level of exports from the Central American countries and Brazil in the first quarter of the calendar year, this came as a surprise to the market, which had been expecting a rise of between 200,000 bags and 350,000 bags," said brokerage GNI in a monthly report.
Producers' front-loading shipments also meant Central American supplies would likely be below normal in the second quarter and keep supply tight.
But Judith Ganes, analyst at Merrill Lynch in New York, said in a biweekly report that Columbia remained the main problem.
Columbia's October-March production was exceptionally low at 5.7 million bags, and the Columbian Coffee Federation hopes April-September output will total 4.5 million bags, Ganes said.
But "based on historical monthly production trends, we have found it might be difficult to achieve this objective and actual (final) output could be as little as 9.4 million bags."

Ganes sees higher coffee prices at least through part of July, barring frost in Brazil. But given supply constraints and expected delays in Columbia's 1997/98 crop, prices could stay firm for September's expiry.
GNI said tight supplies could be offset by a drop in US demand as consumers de-stock but it expected Brazilian "frost-plays" to keep the market tight.
The opposite situation was seen in cocoa as analysts revise up Ivory Coast crop forecasts, which would cut 1996/97's deficit.

Despite an expected 40,000-tonne drop in Brazil's production to 160,000 tonnes, GNI cut its deficit prediction to 33,000 tonnes from 180,000 because of an increase in Ivorian crop estimates to 1.15 million tonnes from 960,000 tonnes.
GNI sees world production at 2.718 million tonnes, versus its last forecast of 2.56 million and 1995/96's 2.856 million.
Local analysts in Abdijan predicted the Ivorian mid-crop (May-Sept) to reach 180,000 tonnes and the main crop (Oct- April) to just exceed a million tonnes.
Cocoa supply scored a 161,000-tonnes surplus last year after the Ivory Coast's record 1.2-million tonnes crop.
Another large Ivorian crop would mean future crops would be expected regularly to surpass 1.2 million tonnes, analysts said.

"Improved crop care by the growers probably had just as much to do with the increased output and therefore, if the practices are continued...there is little reason to believe future harvests will not be as large," Ganes said. She said New York cocoa prices could shed another $50 to $75 per tonne.
Regarding demand, GNI saw consumption rising to 2.751 million tonnes, up from its original estimate of 2.739 million and up 2.1 percent from 1995/96's 2.69 million.
In 1997/98, GNI said, even with 4.0-percent consumption growth, Ivorian and Indonesian production improvements would mean only a modest deficit of about 100,000 tonnes.
Sugar looked broadly balanced in 1996/97 after a near five million-tonnes surplus the year before, GNI said. Production looked roughly on par with last year at 121.2 million tonnes.
It said Australian, Brazilian and European Union gains have been offset by sharply falling India production.
But in 1997/98, GNI said production could fall a million tonnes to 120.2 million.
That, and possible underestimation of demand in populous developing countries, could squeeze sugar next year.
"We anticipate a 2.4-percent rise in 1996/97 offtake to 119.1 million tonnes of raw sugar value and a slightly lower percentage increase in 1997/98 to 121.8 million tonnes," GNI said.

"Growth in consumption is pretty much across the board, but the main danger is that consumption in the populous developing countries such as Brazil, China, Indonesia and Thailand has been underestimated."
GNI estimated a marginal 0.7-million tonne global surplus this year, which could turn into about a 2.1-million deficit in 1997/98.

If the projected deficit for 1997/98 arises, GNI said consumption could close in on 125 million tonnes by 1998/99. "It is our opinion that sugar prices will therefore need to firm to at least 15 cents/pound over the next 12 months to accommodate this need -- even then, it may not be enough," it said.
